title: Google is Having a TPU Moment
summary: Get ready to hear Google brag about TPUs on Wednesday. When Alphabet, Google’s parent company, reports third-quarter earnings tomorrow, the company’s in-house AI chips, tensor processing units, are sure to be on the lips of Google executives and Wall Street analysts. That’s because we got a bunch of new  signs this week of the swelling customer demand for TPUs. Earlier today, Google said that Oracle will become the first major cloud provider outside Google itself to begin offering TPUs to customers through its own data centers. And a short while ago, Ryan Barwick published a scoop for us that says OpenAI—a major customer for Nvidia’s AI chips—plans to buy Google’s TPUs. But perhaps the juiciest details on TPU demand came on Monday courtesy of Anthropic’s IPO prospectus. In that filing, Anthropic chronicled the enormity of the financial commitment it has made to the Google chips, including a plan to spend $114.5 billion with Google Cloud (it didn’t specify how much of that will be for TPU-based compute). Anthropic also estimated it could spend an additional $125 billion to $150 billion on TPUs with Google and other providers. And the AI company will pony up $161.2 billion for TPU compute with Broadcom, which co-designs TPUs with Google. TPUs, you’ll recall, began as chips that Google used only internally starting over a decade ago. The company began allowing outside customers to use them via Google Cloud in 2018. More recently, Google has begun striking agreements with companies like Fluidstack and now Oracle to run TPUs in their own data centers. Google only began recognizing revenue from the sale of TPUs to outside data centers last quarter, though Chief Financial Officer Anat Ashkenazi said on an earnings call then that only a small portion of the revenues from its TPU agreements were reflected during that period. The “vast majority of revenues” from those agreements will kick in next year, Ashkenazi said. Analysts are predicting something of a windfall for Google when that happens. In a report earlier this month, TD Cowen’s John Blackledge estimated that TPUs will generate $9.4 billion in sales during the second half of this year, about 13% of the roughly $70 billion in revenue he was forecasting for Google Cloud during that period. By 2028, Blackledge thinks TPUs could be a $138 billion business, accounting for 34% of Google Cloud’s estimated revenue that year. While big, that figure would still be a fraction of the $692 billion in revenue that analysts, on average, are expecting Nvidia, the dominant provider of AI chips, to report in its fiscal year ending January 2028. Still, Google’s TPU growth has not gone unnoticed at Nvidia. Today, we got further evidence of Nvidia’s efforts to keep marquee companies in its tent. The chipmaker announced an expansion of its partnership with Meta, which said it would increase its deployment of Nvidia chips. As part of the agreement, Nvidia will invest $3 billion into the nearly $100 billion in stock offerings that Meta announced this week. We reported earlier this year that Meta struck a deal to rent TPUs from Google. Nvidia isn’t going to let Google invade its turf without a fight. In Other News Meta increased the size of its planned stock sales to $97.5 billion from $95 billion. The offerings will help the company raise money for its AI investments. Anthropic said it has begun working with Bristol Myers Squibb, BigHat Biosciences and other pharmaceutical companies to use AI in drug discovery. Anthropic also said it acquired a small company, Mithril Medicine, working on treatments for rare forms of muscular dystrophy. Anduril and Qualcomm said they’re working together to build rugged laptops in the U.S. aimed at government, defense, first responders and other customers. The companies are calling the line of computers BlueChip. title: How Is Anthropic So Efficient?
summary: When Anthropic on Monday dropped its long-awaited initial public offering prospectus filing, a lot of the details—see our top takeaways here —weren’t exactly new, given how much my colleagues and others had previously reported about it. Two items stood out to me, though: how Anthropic is running its models more efficiently than before, and changes it made to its already-unusual governance structure. Anthropic’s ability to generate $3.5 billion in free cash flow in the first half of 2026, from $16.3 billion in revenue, shows just how much it has improved the way it runs AI in the cloud, compared to the same period a year earlier, when it burned $1.6 billion. Specifically, Anthropic said it is generating an 85% gross profit margin from powering existing models, which doesn’t include the cost of developing new models. (If that figure rings a bell, it’s the same gross margin estimate my colleague Ann described in this column about Anthropic’s data center grab , which elicited sharp questions from some AI skeptics at the time.) Anthropic is doing so even as it relies almost entirely on computing it rents from cloud providers, which themselves need to generate a profit. So its IPO filing is a reality check on the AI skeptics’ longtime view that a business model founded on selling models on a pay-as-you-go, consumption basis wouldn’t be profitable.

title: Why Cheaper Models Won't Win OpenAI the Enterprise
summary: OpenAI is trying to chip away at Anthropic’s lead with enterprises by fashioning itself as a cheaper, more flexible provider, Steph and I reported this weekend . To be sure, OpenAI has done a great job getting companies like Rippling to switch to its cost-efficient models from Anthropic’s. title: Can AI Help Ray Kurzweil Cheat Death?
summary: Ray Kurzweil does not want to die, but at the age of 78, he has been thinking more about it, a preoccupation that he describes as a “major motivating force of human beings.” So over the past year, Kurzweil, whose keen observations and 2005 bestseller “The Singularity Is Near” have made him one of the most influential prophets of the AI age, has devoted himself to a project to ensure a version of Ray Kurzweil lives on—by creating an AI replica of himself. He calls it Rai. The AI is accessible through a browser on a computer or smartphone. Interacting with it is much like having a Zoom call. Once the AI program is opened, a three-dimensional image of Kurzweil appears against a cosmos-themed backdrop, and it responds to someone’s voice.
